Because the map f is not isomorphic (e.g., since M<N), it will not preserve the ratios of singlet and doublet distributions, i.e., in general ~PDðuÞ= ~PSðuÞsPDðfðuÞÞ=PSðfðuÞÞ. This means that a multiplet state u could appear embedded in one map U1, but neotypic in another map U2. This is easy to appreciate: for example, if analysis is restricted to one subset of genes, then some doublets may be neotypic, while restriction to another subset of genes might cause the same doublets to be embedded. The operational dependence of doublet classiﬁcation on the choice of map f means that the nature of doublet errors cannot be considered to be immutable properties of the doublets. hits.text: Thresholding the Doublet Likelihood In principle, the doublet likelihood L(x) alone could be used to decide on which cells are putative doublets: if hLðxÞi>0:5, call a cell a doublet. The conﬁdence in the call is simply the value of L(x) itself. However, the doublet likelihood L(x) is sensitive to the prior guess, br, on the fraction of observed transcriptomes that are doublets. In practice br is known roughly, but it is easy to be off by several-fold from its true value r. Though uncertainty in br is already used to estimate the error in L(x)i n Equation 8, we should ideally look for a method of doublet classiﬁcation that is not sensitive to br. To do this, we treat L(x) as a feature on which to perform classiﬁcation, rather than as a strict posterior Bayesian probability.
